title: Tax Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy Surcharge Thresholds) Bill 2008

divisions.question: Tax Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy Surcharge Thresholds) Bill 2008 - Second Reading - Put the question

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2008-05-29.34.1) to read the bill for a second time.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through before becoming law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) This means that the majority agree with the main idea of the bill and that the House can now discuss it in more detail. _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r2992) was introduced to increase the [Medicare](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_%28Australia%29) levy surcharge threshold to $100,000 for individuals and to $150,000 for families.(Read more about the bill in its [bills digest](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/billsdgs/T2NQ6/upload_binary/t2nq63.pdf;fileType=application/pdf) (73.8 KB).)

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/debates/?id=2008-05-29.37.1) to read the bill for a third time.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through before becoming law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) This means that the majority agree with the bill and that it will now be sent to the Senate for their consideration. _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r2992) was introduced to increase the [Medicare](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_%28Australia%29) levy surcharge threshold to $100,000 for individuals and to $150,000 for families.(Read more about the bill in its [bills digest](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/billsdgs/T2NQ6/upload_binary/t2nq63.pdf;fileType=application/pdf) (73.8 KB).)
Alan Ferguson The question before the chamber now is that proposed reference No. 2, relating to the Tax Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy Surcharge Thresholds) Bill 2008, be agreed to.
That this bill be now read a second time. That this bill be now read a second time.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, with a motion to proceed without formalities and be read a first time, which was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The speech introduced bills to implement the Montreal Convention for international air carrier liability, strengthen Customs border enforcement and search powers, modernise customs procedures, define tobacco content for duty, and amend the Export Market Development Grants scheme. Key changes include removing the air liability cap with claims up to 100,000 SDR (about A$172,000), and raising the EMDG maximum grant to $200,000, the turnover limit to $50 million, and lowering the expenditure threshold to $10,000.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The opposition moved to refer several government bills to Senate committees for extended inquiry, arguing they required careful scrutiny and were not election policies. The government accused the opposition of economic vandalism, claiming the delays would cost up to $284 million and undermine the budget surplus strategy.
The debate resumed on the luxury car tax bills, with an amendment moved by Senators Bartlett and Nettle to require passage by 24 June 2008 and to omit paragraph (2) of the motion.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the opposition is delaying eight bills through Senate committee referrals without proper justification, including the Same-Sex Relationships (Superannuation) Bill 2008 and the Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Political Donations and Other Measures) Bill 2008. The speaker urged the opposition to support the same‑sex superannuation bill by 1 July, and to pass electoral reforms lowering the donation disclosure threshold to $1,000, banning overseas and anonymous donations, and preventing parties from profiting from public funding.

speeches.speaker: Kerry O'Brien
speeches.brief: The committee report on the Tax Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy Surcharge Thresholds) Bill 2008 and related matters was presented on behalf of Senator Hurley, along with the Hansard record and committee documents.

speeches.speaker: Richard Colbeck
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the bill would cause up to 900,000 people to leave private health insurance, increasing public hospital waiting lists by at least 7% and raising premiums, and noted Treasury’s initial estimate of 485,000 policyholders was revised to 700,000 including dependants.

speeches.speaker: Glenn Sterle
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Tax Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy Surcharge Thresholds) Bill 2008 should be passed to increase the surcharge thresholds from $50,000 to $100,000 for singles and from $100,000 to $150,000 for families, restoring the original intent of targeting high-income earners and providing tax relief to average-income earners. The speaker also criticised the previous Howard government for failing to index the thresholds, which had trapped 465,000 people in an unfair tax, and rejected claims that the change would harm the health system, noting that many people hold cheap insurance only to avoid the levy.

speeches.speaker: Simon Birmingham
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the bill would drive up to one million Australians out of private health insurance, causing a five per cent premium increase and shifting $2.7 billion in costs to public hospitals, and urged its defeat.

speeches.speaker: David Bushby
speeches.brief: The bill to increase Medicare levy surcharge thresholds from $50,000 to $100,000 for singles and from $100,000 to $150,000 for families was opposed, with the argument that it would cause up to one million people to drop private health insurance, remove $2.7 billion from hospital funding, and increase public hospital waiting lists.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Conroy
speeches.brief: The bill raised the Medicare levy surcharge thresholds to $75,000 for singles and $150,000 for couples, with annual indexation, as a compromise after consultations with figures including Liberal senators Colbeck and Cormann, the Australian Private Hospitals Association, Access Economics, and Terry Barnes.
